The capsule is pinned to a flat surface (luminal side up) and fixed overnight in neutral buffered formalin (Figure 16A). Findings such as fibrinous or necrotic material on the inner capsule surface, irregularities, and/or wall thickenings must be sampled. Because of the multifocality of BIA-ALCL, adequate and thorough sampling is required. For the optimal handling of these specimens, it is recommended that at least two random sections of each of the six aspects of the capsule (anterior, posterior, media

erial rather than tissue sections [169]. The neoplastic cells in the fluid may be scant or numerous and intermingled with fibrinoid and necrotic material and with small lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells [171]. The neoplastic cells are large (4–5X larger than a small lymphocyte) with significant atypia and may have cytoplasmic vacuoles. The nucleus is usually bilobed and hyperchromatic, with prominent nucleoli. In some cases, however, the nucleus is markedly displaced to the periphery to resemble a signet-ring cell. “Hallmark” cells are seen in up to two-thirds of cases (Figure 16B,C).

The immunophenotype of the lymphoma cells is identical to ALK- ALCL and pc ALCL. BIA-ALCL cells are strongly positive for CD30, variably positive for CD45, and are negative for ALK (Figure 16D and Figure 17B–D). The neoplastic cells are variably positive for EMA, CD4, CD43, and TIA-1 as well as for the T-cell markers CD2, CD3, and CD45RO, while negative for CD20, PAX5, and CD68 [30]. Strong positivity for CD30 is very useful to confirm the diagnosis both in a cell block and while observing the luminal side of a capsule, particularly at the early stages (T1-T2, see below). Nuclear pSTAT3 expression, consistent with the molecular biology of the tumor, is also remarkable. EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER) and LMP1 are negative. panels.figure_caption: a Ultrasound revealed a large septated seroma (white arrow), which was aspirated the following day. Cytology confirmed BIA-ALCL. Ultrasound has a sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 75% for detecting an effusion. These figures are similar or better than CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in effusion detection [7]. b MRI provides characterisation of the implant’s capsule, defining enhancement and thickening [14, 15]. This makes it the modality of choice for defining the implant capsule (white arrow) [7]. BIA-ALCL typically presents as a delayed, non-infective fluid collection surrounding the implant (red arrow) or its surrounding scar capsule, with or without evidence of capsular rupture [13]. c Staging CT revealed a small to moderate effusion adjacent to both breast implants (white arrows)
in_text_mentions: th a sudden and rapid increase in the size of her left breast. The patient had bilateral textured breast implants inserted 4 years previously. The patient was referred for ultrasound assessment (Fig. 3a).Fig. 3a Ultrasound revealed a large septated seroma (white arrow), which was aspirated the following day. Cytology confirmed BIA-ALCL. The patient underwent MRI assessment (Fig. 3b). The external structure of the implant has been found to statistically influence the risk of developing BIA-ALCL, with the majority of cases occurring with textured breast implants [13]. There has been no significant difference in incidence between saline and silicone implants. There is also inadequate evidence to comment if implant location plays a role in developing BIA-ALCL [5].

The patient was staged with CT (Fig. 3c). Many patients with BIA-ALCL have an effusion, mass or lymphadenopathy on CT evaluation [14]. Other findings can include irregularity of implant contour and capsular thickening [10, 14, 15]. The patient underwent bilateral implant removal, with bilateral capsulectomies. Subsequent PET/CT showed complete metabolic remission. Surprisingly, the patient had bilateral breast implantations the following year, despite being warned of the risk of BIA-ALCL recurrence. The patient is being closely monitored for evidence of relapse.

Patients with BIA-ALCL often present to their primary clinician with breast enlargement, asymmetry, skin rash, contracture or lymphadenopathy [8]. The average time frame of presentation is 7 years following breast implantation [1]. Initial presentation often manifests as a peri-prosthetic effusion surrounding an implant on ultrasound. Any new effusion around an implant of more than 12 months of age should prompt consideration of BIA-ALCL. Patient A subsequently underwent ultrasound assessment (Fig. 1b).

y of BIA-ALCL is an effusion in relation to the breast implant [7]. These can be peri-prosthetic or even present in the subcutaneous layer [9]. Aspirated fluid must be sent for flow cytometry and not simply for microscopy and culture, with the pathologist alerted to the possibility of the BIA-ALCL. If ultrasound examination is indeterminate, then magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) should be considered for further evaluation (Fig. 1c). The patient was subsequently admitted for implant removal with capsulectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 8 panels (EE 2.5x, EE 40x, CD30, ALK1, EMA, CD4, TIA1, Perforin). EE 2.5x: Low-power H&E showing breast parenchyma and periprosthetic capsule, consistent with BIA-ALCL. EE 40x: High-power H&E showing large atypical blasts characteristic of BIA-ALCL. CD30: CD30 immunostain showing strong positivity in neoplastic cells, typical of BIA-ALCL. ALK1: ALK1 immunostain showing negativity, consistent with ALK-negative BIA-ALCL. EMA: EMA immunostain showing positivity in neoplastic cells, a characteristic feature of BIA-ALCL. CD4: CD4 immunostain showing positivity, typical of BIA-ALCL. TIA1: TIA-1 immunostain showing positivity, consistent with cytotoxic phenotype of BIA-ALCL. Perforin: Perforin immunostain showing positivity, supporting cytotoxic phenotype of BIA-ALCL.

panels.figure_caption: Histology and immunohistochemistry of Case #2. Breast parenchyma and periprosthetic capsule are shown. The presence of sheets of large atypical blasts with irregular nuclear contours, coarse chromatin and evident nucleoli can be observed. The lymphoid cells are surrounded by fi-brinous material with only scattered atypical large neoplastic cells. Immuno-histochemically, the neoplastic cells are diffusely positive for CD30, CD4, EMA, TIA-1, and Perforin stains while they are consistently negative for ALK-1 stain. Scale bar of the top left image: 0.5 cm; other scale bars: 20 µm.
in_text_mentions: At morphology, the cells were four to five times larger than a mature lymphocyte, with a much more eosinophilic and granular cytoplasm. In this case, the cytoplasmic vacuoles were so abundant that, combining together, gave the neoplastic cells a signet ring appearance (Figure 6) [10]. Moreover, cellular outlines demonstrate cytoplasmic fragmentation. This morphology has also been described by Hu et al. [36]. Immunohistochemically, the neoplastic cells were diffusely positive for CD30, CD4, CD15, EMA, TIA-1, and Perforin. ALK-1, CD3, CD20, and PAX5 stains were consistently negative (Figure 7).

Strong membranous expression of CD30 in the neoplastic cells (200×); in-text confirms no ALK expression

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Low-power H&E of core-needle biopsy showing fibrous tissue fragments with dense lymphoid foci; the caption and in-text confirm this is the BIA-ALCL case, representing lymphoid involvement of the peri-implant fibrous capsule. b: High-power H&E showing the dense infiltrate composed of large atypical lymphoid cells with eosinophils, a classic morphologic feature of BIA-ALCL on the core-needle biopsy of the confirmed case. c: Oil-immersion H&E showing hallmark cells with kidney-shaped nuclei, the textbook cytologic hallmark of ALCL, in tissue from the confirmed BIA-ALCL patient. d: Immunohistochemistry panel showing strong membranous CD30 positivity in the neoplastic cells; the in-text immunophenotype (CD30 positive, ALK negative) supports the CD30-positive ALK-negative BIA-ALCL phenotype.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: High-power H&E showing hallmark (horseshoe) cells with eccentric nuclei amid a mixed infiltrate, the classic cytomorphology of anaplastic large cell lymphoma; in-text confirms biopsy and peri-implant fluid cytology established CD30+/ALK- ALCL in a breast-implant patient. b: CD30 immunostain with diffuse strong positivity in the large lymphoma cells, a defining immunophenotype of BIA-ALCL; in-text confirms CD30+/ALK- anaplastic large cell lymphoma. c: ALK immunostain diffusely negative, completing the CD30+/ALK- immunophenotype characteristic of breast implant-associated ALCL; in-text confirms CD30+/ALK- anaplastic large cell lymphoma.

panels.figure_caption: High power (40x) of horseshoe cells (cells with eccentric nuclei) with a mixed infiltrate in between, which are the “hallmarks cells” in anaplastic lymphoma (a), lymphoma/large cells shown diffusely positive for CD30 (b), and ALK shown diffusely negative throughout (c).
in_text_mentions: iple lesions in the right breast, the largest measuring up to 5 cm with SUV ranging from 10 to 52.4 (Figure 2) and two hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the right axilla measuring 1.7 and 3.7 cm with SUV of 6.0 and 15.8, respectively (Figure 2). There was also a hypermetabolic band posterior to the implant involving the pectoralis minor muscle measuring 5 × 1 cm with an SUV of 33.7 (Figure 2). Bone marrow biopsy was not performed. The biopsies of the breast, right axillary lymph nodes, and fluid cytology surrounding the breast capsule confirmed CD30+/ALK− anaplastic large cell lymphoma (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel a shows H&E-stained cell block material from a peri-prosthesis effusion aspirate with medium to large discohesive atypical cells, irregular hyperchromatic nuclei, peripherally-located horseshoe-shaped nuclei, and atypical mitoses — the classic cytomorphologic hallmark of BIA-ALCL in seroma fluid. The inset white box marks the atypical mitosis, confirming an annotation. b: Panel b comprises four immunohistochemical stains (CD3, CD30, ALK1, Ki-67) performed on cell block material from the peri-implant fluid collection. Diffuse CD30 positivity with ALK1 negativity is the classic immunophenotype of BIA-ALCL. The high Ki-67 labeling index (>80%) supports the diagnosis. Each sub-image is labeled with its antibody name.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histopathology (100x) of the left breast capsule from a patient with BIA-ALCL, showing clusters of large pleomorphic neoplastic cells adjacent to luminal fibrinoid necrosis with a mixed inflammatory background. The article title, caption, and in-text diagnostic statement confirm breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma. Real human patient tissue showing a specific diagnostic manifestation of the target disease. B: High-power H&E inset (1000x) of the same breast capsule specimen showing the classic hallmark cells of BIA-ALCL: pleomorphic large neoplastic cells with eccentric horseshoe- and kidney-shaped nuclei. The caption and in-text diagnostic statement confirm this is breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma. Real human patient histopathology showing a specific diagnostic cytomorphologic feature of the target disease.
panels.attribution_text: Ezekwudo et al. Breast Implant-Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.. Case reports in oncological medicine 2017. doi:10.1155/2017/6478467. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Representative sections of the left breast capsule. Larger image: the capsule contains small lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells, and occasional eosinophils. In addition, there are clusters of large neoplastic cells throughout the capsule, adjacent to the luminal fibrinoid necrosis (hematoxylin and eosin, 100x). Inset image: the large neoplastic cells are pleomorphic with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant clear to slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. Occasional “hallmark” cells with eccentric horseshoe- and kidney-shaped nuclei (hematoxylin and eosin, 1000x).
in_text_mentions: east capsule showed fibrin deposition with a thin row of highly atypical cells. The atypical cells were large and pleomorphic, with hyperchromatic nuclei and occasional prominent nucleoli noted along with abundant clear to slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm (Figure 4). Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated strong CD30, CD43, and MUM1 expression, while EMA was weakly positive (Figure 5). The cells did not express ALK (Figure 5), CD20, CD79a, or estrogen receptor. The overall morphology and immunohistochemical profile were diagnostic for breast implant–associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma.

in_text_mentions: A 41-year-old white female patient presented with a 6-week history of spontaneous unilateral breast swelling, pain, and an intramammary itching of her left breast. She had undergone bilateral breast augmentation using textured round high profile gel breast implants with a volume of 535cc six years ago in Hungary. She reported smoking three cigarettes daily. The patient has a positive family history for breast cancer on her maternal side. Her cup size was 80G and her BMI was 27.3. On physical examination, her left breast was noted to be swollen in comparison to the right (Figure 1).

(a) Section illustrating large, pleomorphic cells with occasional horseshoe-shaped nuclei (hematoxylin and eosin stain; magnification: 400×). (e) The blasts are positive for CD4 (magnification: 200×). (f) The cells are strongly positive for CD30 (magnification: 200×).
in_text_mentions: Histological examination revealed a capsule with multiple nodular distensions (Figure 6a). Within these nodules, sparsely arranged blastic cells are organized in aggregates, characterized by oval, kidney-shaped nuclei. The background includes small, chromatin-dense lymphocytes, individual plasma cells, histiocytes, and eosinophilic granulocytes. In some areas, the infiltration extends to within fractions of a millimeter from the muscle (Figure 6b). The cells are uniformly negative for ALK and CD3 but positive for CD4 and CD30 (Figure 6c–f). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E of the breast implant capsule from a confirmed BIA-ALCL case showing the fibrous capsule with reactive lymphoid aggregates; part of the diagnostic capsular pathology of the disease. B: High-power H&E showing atypical large cells with hyperchromatic nuclei in the capsular stroma, the hallmark anaplastic cells of BIA-ALCL in this confirmed case. C: CD30 immunohistochemistry positive at the luminal side of the capsule, the classic immunophenotype of BIA-ALCL, with the caption stating pathologic stage T1. D: ALK immunohistochemistry negative in the atypical cells, confirming the CD30-positive ALK-negative immunophenotype diagnostic of BIA-ALCL in this case.

panels.figure_caption: (A) A bland fibrous capsule is identified, with occasional reactive lymphoid aggregates (arrow) (H&E, ×10). (B) The stroma demonstrates lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration, accompanied by scattered atypical cells with large, hyperchromatic nuclei (H&E, ×40). (C) Immunohistochemical staining shows CD30 at the luminal side, consistent with pathologic stage T1 (IHC, ×20). (D) Immunohistochemical staining for ALK is negative in the atypical cells (IHC, ×20).
in_text_mentions: Postoperative immunohistochemical analysis was performed on the capsular tissues of both breast implants. The results demonstrated that the atypical lymphoid cells in the right implant capsule tissue showed positivity for CD30, CD4, and EMA, and negativity for ALK, with no evidence of extracapsular extension, findings consistent with the pathological diagnosis of BIA-ALCL (Figure 2). On the left side, no definitive malignancy was identified. All surgical margins were negative postoperatively. The final diagnosis was reviewed and confirmed by an experienced hematopathologist at our institution.

in_text_mentions: east capsule showed fibrin deposition with a thin row of highly atypical cells. The atypical cells were large and pleomorphic, with hyperchromatic nuclei and occasional prominent nucleoli noted along with abundant clear to slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm (Figure 4). Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated strong CD30, CD43, and MUM1 expression, while EMA was weakly positive (Figure 5). The cells did not express ALK (Figure 5), CD20, CD79a, or estrogen receptor. The overall morphology and immunohistochemical profile were diagnostic for breast implant–associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma.

panels.rationale: Gross specimen photograph from a BIA-ALCL case report: explanted capsulectomy specimen inner surface with fibrin deposits (black arrows) and the intact mammary implant from the same patient. The caption confirms CD30-positive, ALK-negative tumor cells on the capsule surface, the defining immunophenotype of BIA-ALCL, making disease attribution strong. The visible thickened fibrinous capsular lining is a classic gross manifestation of the peri-implant inflammatory process in BIA-ALCL. No panel letters exist in the image or caption, so it is treated as a single-image figure (panel A).

Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI revealed a periprosthetic fluid collection and mass-like enhancement on the left breast at the 4 o'clock region showing sustained peripheral enhancement (Figure 1). Family history: the father died of colon cancer. Fluid was aspirated, and cytologic smears on a tissue block were analyzed by hematoxylin-eosin stain and immunohistochemistry. The tumor cells were positive for CD45, CD3, and CD30. Additionally, CD68 was positive in a population of reactive background histiocytes. plate_findings.evidence: Fine needle cytology: neoplastic proliferation of large round cells with pleomorphic nuclei, negative for epithelial marker CK (A)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Fine-needle cytology immunostain panel from a BIA-ALCL case report patient; panel A shows the neoplastic proliferation of large round cells with pleomorphic nuclei staining negative for the epithelial marker CK, consistent with an anaplastic large cell population of lymphoid (non-epithelial) lineage, matching the captioned and in-text ALK-negative ALCL diagnosis. [raw subtype: ALK-negative] B: Companion immunostained cytology field of the same patient showing the large pleomorphic neoplastic cells positive for the lymphoid marker CD45 and vimentin, confirming the ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma diagnosis stated in the article for Figures 2A, B. [raw subtype: ALK-negative]

in_text_mentions: o-pectoral lymph nodes (SUV max 7.8; dmt max 26 mm). Clinical and radiographic evaluations of the right breast did not show any abnormalities. The patient was subjected to fine needle aspiration of mass; cytology exam showed round, large cells with pleomorphic and cerebroid nuclei (CD45+++, Vimentin++, Keratin−). The following percutaneous biopsy of the mass demonstrated a proliferation of phenotypically aberrant population of large cells that expressed CD30 and CD45, negative for CD3, CD20, and ALK1, diagnostic for anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-negative (ALK-ALCL) ( Figures 2A, B ) (8).

panels.rationale: Real-patient axial breast MRI from a case report titled 'Breast Implant-Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma'. The caption documents smooth circumferential thickening of the right implant fibrous capsule with diffuse progressive enhancement, and the in-text for this same MRI describes a moderate peri-implant fluid collection between capsule and implant shell with a folded shell and no rupture - i.e., a late peri-implant seroma, the hallmark imaging presentation of BIA-ALCL. The left capsule is normal, providing an internal comparison, but the panel as a whole shows the pathologic right side. Disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title plus the specific captioned manifestations. No arrows or callouts mark the findings (only MRI technical overlays and a laterality marker), so annotations_present is false. No age or ethnicity stated; MRI does not permit Fitzpatrick skin-tone assessment.

panels.rationale: Single-panel bilateral breast MRI from a BIA-ALCL case report. The caption and in-text explicitly state the MRI confirms left-breast edema/fluid accumulation around the left subpectoral silicone implant — a late peri-implant seroma, the classic radiologic presentation of BIA-ALCL. The image is dark but the bilateral implants and peri-implant fluid are discernible, and the prior caption triage kept it as a real patient radiology image. No arrows or annotations are present. Subtype left null because the provided vocabulary does not define BIA-ALCL subtypes; skin tone and ethnicity are not assessable/stated.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Axial PET-CT showing a pathologically enlarged, FDG-avid left axillary lymph node in a patient with BIA-ALCL; the in-text confirms fine needle aspiration of the left axillary node was consistent with high-grade lymphoma, establishing this as a specific manifestation of the target disease. Real human-patient radiology; no vocabulary key exists for nodal PET uptake, so the finding is proposed. b: Axial PET-CT showing metabolically active peri-implant seroma with capsular thickening around the left breast implant — the classic imaging presentation of BIA-ALCL in this patient, directly matching the caption and the disease-focused article title.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (EE 40X, CD30, ALK, CD7, CD15, EMA, Perforin (inset)). EE 40X: Cytology smear from the peri-implant seroma of a BIA-ALCL case (Case #3) showing the atypical large cells described in the caption; article title and text confirm the diagnosis of BIA-ALCL. CD30: CD30 immunostain of the neoplastic cells in Case #3 BIA-ALCL, the hallmark diagnostic immunophenotype. ALK: ALK-1 stain from the same BIA-ALCL case; negativity is part of the diagnostic CD30+/ALK- phenotype stated in the caption and confirmed in the text. CD7: CD7 immunostain of the BIA-ALCL neoplastic cells with weak/partial positivity, as stated in caption and text (Figure 9). CD15: CD15 immunostain shows positivity of the neoplastic cells in this BIA-ALCL case, as stated in the caption and text. EMA: EMA immunostain of the same BIA-ALCL case; caption states negativity, part of the reported immunophenotypic work-up. Perforin (inset): Perforin immunostain inset within the EMA panel showing...
panels.attribution_text: Davanzo et al. Flow Cytometry Analysis in Breast Implant-Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma: Three Case Reports.. International journal of molecular sciences 2024. doi:10.3390/ijms25063518. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 9.
panels.figure_caption: Cytology and immunohistochemistry of Case #3 cytoinclusions. Predominantly amorphous, sparsely cellular material including rare neutrophilic granulocytes, macrophages, small lymphocytes, and isolated atypical large elements. Immunohistochemically, the neoplastic cells are positive for CD30 and CD15 stains and negative for ALK-1 and EMA stains. CD7 stain is weakly/partially positive; Perforin is partially positive. Scale bar: 40 µm.
in_text_mentions: The cytological examination revealed the presence of rare cells, not suggesting per se the presence of lymphoproliferative disorders. Only after knowledge of the FCM results, targeted immunohistochemical analysis was performed, which confirmed the diagnosis of BIA-ALCL. Atypical cells were positive for CD30, CD4, CD15, and Perforin and negative for ALK-1, CD3, CD8, CD2, EMA, CD20, and PAX5. CD7 was weakly/partially positive (doubtful positivity) (Figure 9).

in_text_mentions: The sections of the left breast capsule/mastopexy tissue and breast implant showed fibrous tissue with large pleomorphic tumor cells lining the inner surface of the capsule as a distinct layer caught in a fibrinoid and highly necrotic meshwork. Focally, small clusters of tumor cells superficially penetrated the capsule and the fibrous tissue beyond. There was a strong CD30 expression on the tumor cells lining the capsule. In some of the foci, the CD30+ lymphoma cells extended superficially into the underlying fibrous tissue (Figures 5-8).

panels.rationale: Single-panel cytology image of peri-implant seroma fluid showing anaplastic large cells, the hallmark manifestation of breast implant-associated ALCL. The article title, caption ('Effusion fluid (seroma). Anaplastic large cells present in the effusion surrounding the breast implant'), and in-text mention (ALK-negative ALCL in cystic fluid) directly attribute this panel to breast_implant_associated_alcl. The caption additionally notes IHC confirms T-cell type and the in-text states ALK-negative, supporting the subtype. Patient was staged Ann Arbor stage IIE per in-text. No age or ethnicity stated; no skin shown; no annotations present. [raw subtype: ALK-negative, T-cell type]

Bone marrow analysis was performed and showed no evidence of lymphoma involvement. The patient was staged as Ann Arbor stage IIE. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Ultrasound panel showing large peri-implant fluid collection with thick septations and solid detritus adjacent to saline implant, the classic sonographic presentation of BIA-ALCL. B: Second ultrasound view of the same peri-implant fluid collection with detritus, classic for BIA-ALCL seroma. C: Power Doppler ultrasound demonstrating avascular peri-implant fluid collection, supporting seroma rather than vascularized mass; classic BIA-ALCL finding. D: MRI STIR sequence showing peri-implant fluid collection with solid detritus surrounding the implant, confirming the seroma seen on ultrasound; classic BIA-ALCL manifestation. E: Postcontrast MRI showing a 2.3 cm irregular enhancing peri-implant capsular mass, a recognized but less common manifestation of BIA-ALCL than seroma. F: T1 Fat Sat postcontrast MRI showing prominent level 1 axillary lymph node without fatty hilum; lymph node involvement can occur in BIA-ALCL but is less...

panels.figure_caption: Breast implant‐associated anaplastic large‐cell lymphoma. Radiology. Ultrasound demonstrates a large fluid collection which contains thick septations and solid detritus (arrows) adjacent to the saline implant (A, B), with no evidence of vascularity on Power Doppler imaging (C). Axial MRI STIR sequence obtained in the prone position demonstrates the peri‐implant fluid collection with solid detritus (arrows) surrounding the implant (I) (D). Postcontrast subtraction axial sequence demonstrates a 2.3 cm irregular enhancing mass along the medial aspect of the right implant (arrow) (E). T1 Fat Sat with contrast demonstrates a prominent level 1 axillary lymph node without fatty hilum (F). Second look ultrasound confirmed the presence of the mass that was identified deep to the implant in the supine position (G).

The red arrow marks a simple anechoic peri-implant fluid collection (seroma) superficial to the intact implant, the classic sonographic manifestation of BIA-ALCL. Disease attribution is strong: the article is specifically about breast implant-associated ALCL and the in-text states the aspirated seroma fluid showed seroma-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK-negative). Only the peri-implant seroma finding is visible on this ultrasound; cytology/IHC/MRI/capsular findings are not depicted. No age, ethnicity, or stage is stated. [raw subtype: seroma-associated]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: T2 MRI shows a peri-implant seroma with internal septations, a classic BIA-ALCL imaging manifestation; article is a case report of BIA-ALCL. B: Post-contrast T1 MRI shows only minimal peripheral enhancement of the peri-implant collection capsule wall; this is part of the BIA-ALCL case imaging but is less specific than the seroma itself. C: Post-contrast T1 MRI demonstrates a prominent left axillary lymph node with cortical thickening in a patient with BIA-ALCL; axillary lymphadenopathy is a recognized but less specific finding.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph (panel A) from a case report of locally advanced breast implant-associated anaplastic large-cell lymphoma. It shows the presenting physical-examination appearance of the patient: firmness and marked asymmetric enlargement of the right breast, the classic late presentation of BIA-ALCL associated with recurrent peri-implant seroma. Prior caption triage confirms a real patient image with no third-party restriction. The unilateral breast enlargement vocabulary key is directly supported by the caption and the visible asymmetry; the seroma-specific ultrasound finding key is not applied because this is a physical-exam photograph, not an ultrasound.

She developed a recurrent fluid collection involving her right breast (Figure 1). A drain was placed and yielded minimal output before being removed 1 week later.
